claims.text: Friction stir repair is a solid-state joining technique.
Friction stir repair will reduce hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
Friction stir repair will preserve microstructural integrity and mechanical performance under aggressive operating conditions.
Certain high-entropy alloys can possess microstructures susceptible to hot cracking during fusion welding.
The susceptible material contains high-melting-point phases.
Friction stir repair can be performed while maintaining the processed material below its melting temperature.
Friction stir repair produces a refined, ultrafine microstructure in the stir zone.
The stir-zone microstructure avoids formation of low-melting intergranular films.
Avoiding low-melting intergranular films improves mechanical continuity and reduces crack susceptibility.
Operating in the solid state prevents the localized melting and rapid solidification associated with fusion welding.
Low-melting liquid or second-phase material in interdendritic or grain-boundary regions contributes to hot-crack initiation during solidification.
Plastic deformation and controlled heat input during friction stir repair promote dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization produces a homogeneous microstructure with enhanced ductility.
Friction-stir-repaired components will exhibit fewer or no hot-cracking defects and better cracking resistance under thermal and mechanical stress than fusion-welded repairs.
Fusion welding can create hot cracking through solidification shrinkage and the presence of a low-melting interdendritic phase.
The anticipated benefit depends on controlling friction stir parameters to avoid full melting and on keeping thermal and mechanical loads within the performance limits of the refined microstructure.
